description: DEF CON 33 Adversary Village — 10 talks from the canonical playlist covering purple teaming, threat emulation, supply chain risks, adversary tradecraft, and cyber economics.

talks.title: Redefining Purple Teaming for Max Impact
talks.teaser: How modern security teams transition from siloed operations to unified, intelligence-driven purple teaming.
talks.summary:
Introduction and Evolution of Purple Teaming

Adam Pennington (lead of MITRE ATT&CK at MITRE Corporation), Sydney Marrone (Principal Threat Hunter and Purple Team lead at Splunk), and Lauren Proehl (Global Head of Detection & Response at Marsh McLennan and co-founder of Thor Collective) host a panel on transforming purple teaming from an occasional exercise into a continuous, high-impact operational program. Traditionally, security organizations operated with stark boundaries between offensive red teams and defensive blue teams, resulting in adversarial relationships and siloed findings. The panel explores how contemporary purple teaming unites both disciplines around shared threat intelligence, iterative adversary emulation, and concrete detection engineering.

Core Philosophy: Breaking Down Red and Blue Silos

The panel emphasizes that purple teaming is not merely a scheduled meeting or a one-off assessment, but a collaborative mindset and operational loop. Rather than celebrating red team triumphs or scrutinizing blue team misses, purple teaming creates a safe, blame-free environment where operators execute specific adversary techniques while defenders observe telemetry, alert pipelines, and log collection in real time. This immediate feedback loop allows teams to tune detection rules, address visibility gaps, and validate defensive controls on the spot.

Scoping and Executing Purple Team Exercises

The speakers outline practical methodologies for scoping and running exercises across organizations with varying maturity levels:

Starting in Isolated Environments: When introducing purple teaming to risk-averse organizations, start within dedicated virtual labs or staging environments equipped with production EDR agents and logging pipelines. Demonstrating tangible improvements in a non-disruptive sandbox builds management trust.

Establishing Clear Rules of Engagement: Define explicit guardrails, target systems, and acceptable techniques prior to execution, ensuring management and system owners understand the scope and intent of the assessment.

Iterative Cadence: Rather than conducting single massive annual exercises, conduct focused, frequent exercises targeting specific threat actors, platforms, or attack phases.

Threat-Informed Defense vs. Blue Sky Emulation

A central discussion centers on balancing intelligence-driven adversary emulation against open-ended exploratory testing. While threat intelligence provides rich telemetry for well-documented threat groups (such as APT28 or APT29) in enterprise environments, specialized domains (like operational technology or cloud infrastructure) often have limited public threat data. In mature organizations or specialized sectors, practitioners should pair threat-informed baseline testing with creative, exploratory techniques to uncover unexpected blind spots.

Managing Risk and Organizational Buy-In

Securing executive support requires shifting the narrative from technical exploit metrics to business resilience. By demonstrating measurable gains—such as reduced mean time to detect, verified telemetry pipelines, and closed coverage gaps—purple teams prove their ROI. The panelists advise starting with small, high-confidence wins before seeking approval for more complex scenarios such as live helpdesk social engineering or production infrastructure emulation.

The Role of AI and Future Outlook

The panelists examine how emerging technologies and AI are influencing adversary emulation and threat hunting. While fully autonomous, agentic adversary simulation remains in development, current AI tools significantly lower the barrier to entry by assisting blue teamers with script translation, technique research, and rapid hypothesis generation during hunts.

Key Takeaways and Practical Guidance

Cultivate Collaboration: Purple teaming succeeds when red and blue operators share context openly without ego or fear of failure.

Iterate Incrementally: Build momentum through targeted, repeatable exercises rather than sprawling, infrequent engagements.

Leverage Open Frameworks: Utilize established standards like MITRE ATT&CK and open emulation plans to ground testing in realistic adversary behaviors.

talks.title: Thinking Like an Attacker Is No Longer Optional
talks.teaser: Why defenders must adopt an adversarial mindset and embed offensive thinking to build true resilience.
talks.summary:
Introduction: The Necessity of an Adversarial Mindset

Moderated by Abhijith 'Abx' B R (founder of Adversary Village) alongside Keenan Skelly, this expert panel features Bryson Bort (founder of SCYTHE and GRIMM, co-founder of the ICS Village), Anant Shrivastava (founder of Cyfinoid Research), and Lieutenant Colonel Gordon Baum ("Fizzle", US Air Force 567th Cyberspace Operations Group). The panel addresses why passive, compliance-driven defenses inevitably fail against modern threat actors and makes the case for systematically embedding offensive adversarial thinking across organizational security programs.

Distinguishing the Hacker Mindset from the Adversary Mindset

The panel delineates the crucial differences between a generic hacker mindset and a strategic adversary mindset:

Hacker Mindset: Characterized by intellectual curiosity, technical exploration, and exploiting technical quirks in isolation.

Adversary Mindset: Driven by strategic mission objectives, economics, planning, and persistence. Real-world adversaries are not lone hobbyists operating in a vacuum; they operate with defined mission parameters, budgets, timelines, and logistical constraints. Adversaries prioritize the path of least resistance—whether through physical close-access operations, social engineering, or abusing misconfigured trust relationships—rather than exclusively pursuing complex zero-day exploits.

The Evolution of Offensive Security and Moving Beyond Ego

Bryson Bort highlights how offensive security has matured over the last decade. Historically, penetration testing and red teaming were frequently dominated by adversarial ego, where operators sought to breach Domain Admin, drop a brief technical report, and move on without providing actionable remediation guidance. Modern offensive security must focus on partnership with defenders, measuring success by how effectively the engagement improves detection visibility and defensive resilience.

Breach and Attack Simulation vs. Critical Thinking

The panel evaluates automated Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS) platforms versus human-led adversarial testing. While automated BAS platforms provide consistent regression testing and baseline telemetry, tools cannot replace human critical thinking, contextual analysis, and creative pivoting. Tools exist to support organizational processes, governance, and people—not to replace strategic judgment.

Prioritizing Defense: From Vulnerability Assessment to Red Teaming

Anant Shrivastava and Gordon Baum discuss the practical stages of building an offensive-informed defensive posture:

Foundational Hygiene First: Organizations must establish basic asset inventory and vulnerability management before rushing into complex simulation exercises. Handing an immature team a list of thousands of simulated attack findings creates paralysis.

Graduated Progression: Organizations should progress systematically from vulnerability scanning and penetration testing to purple teaming, and ultimately to full-scope red teaming.

Contrarian Perspective: Adversarial thinkers introduce contrarian viewpoints, challenging organizational assumptions regarding which assets are critical and how trust boundaries interact.

The Role of Open-Source Tools and Practical Purple Teaming

Defenders do not require multimillion-dollar budgets to adopt offensive thinking. Free and open-source tools—such as Atomic Red Team or PowerShell-based execution scripts—allow blue teams to generate reliable adversarial signals and test log ingestion pipelines immediately. Collaborative purple teaming aligns teams across scoping, execution, and validation.

Key Takeaways for Modern Defenders

Security is a Critical Thinking Discipline: No tool or AI platform can replace contextual human analysis and threat understanding.

Adopt Adversary Economics: Understand what threat actors want and how they calculate risk, cost, and opportunity when targeting your environment.

Collaborate Continuously: Bridge the divide between offensive researchers and frontline defenders to turn vulnerability discovery into long-term defensive resilience.

talks.title: How Malicious Packages on npm Bypass Existing Security Tools
talks.teaser: Why conventional SCA, SAST, and EDR tools fail against malicious npm packages and how attackers exploit registries.
talks.summary:
Introduction to the npm Threat Landscape

Paul McCarty, Head of Research at Safe-T and seasoned supply chain security researcher, delivers an in-depth technical analysis of open-source malware within the npm ecosystem. As the world's largest software registry hosting nearly 5 million packages and serving over 4.5 trillion package requests in 2024, npm has become the primary vector for software supply chain attacks. Industry telemetry indicates that over 98% of malicious open-source packages are hosted and delivered through npm due to its frictionless publishing model and ubiquitous developer integration.

Why Traditional Security Tools Fail Against Supply Chain Attacks

McCarty dissects why standard enterprise security controls fail to detect or block malicious npm packages:

Software Composition Analysis (SCA): SCA solutions operate by cross-referencing package names and versions against public vulnerability databases (such as CVEs and NVD). Malicious packages created by threat actors do not contain reported CVEs; they are intentionally authored malware, making them completely invisible to standard SCA scanners.

Static Application Security Testing (SAST): SAST engines are designed to locate programmer errors, input sanitization flaws, or memory vulnerabilities in source code, not purposeful obfuscated malware payloads or lifecycle install scripts.

Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and Antivirus: Package installation scripts (such as preinstall or postinstall hooks) run during build or developer setup. Payloads often execute as single-shot commands (e.g. curl or node execution) that immediately exfiltrate environment variables or spawn background processes without triggering heuristic behavior chains monitored by endpoint agents.

Attack Vectors in the Open-Source Ecosystem

Threat actors exploit various vectors to deliver malware to developer workstations and CI/CD pipelines:

Typosquatting and Dependency Confusion: Registering package names identical to internal corporate packages or mimicking popular public libraries to trick build systems into fetching public malware.

Obfuscation and Filler Code: Embedding malicious logic deep inside thousands of lines of dummy JavaScript files and nested dependencies to evade manual code review and automated AST parsers.

Conditional Execution: Writing payloads that only activate when specific cryptographic wallet files, environment keys, or enterprise domain flags are detected, remaining completely dormant in sandboxes.

Threat Actor Case Studies: Nation-States and Criminal Groups

McCarty details several active campaigns targeting the npm ecosystem:

North Korean Threat Groups (Lazarus / DPRK): Responsible for billions in cryptocurrency theft, these actors conduct targeted social engineering on LinkedIn and GitHub, distributing fake technical challenges and dependencies with dormant stealers that target developer crypto wallets.

Indonesian Threat Groups ("Len Gang"): Groups targeting WhatsApp web integrations and business accounts to hijack payment systems, utilizing Discord webhooks for effortless command and control infrastructure.

Russian Underground Actors: Increased utilization of .ru and .su top-level domains for payload hosting, adapting infrastructure to evade sanctions.

The Bug Bounty Problem and Ecosystem Pollution

A major contributor to registry pollution is the deluge of reckless bug bounty researchers. Over 40% of newly uploaded suspicious packages stem from researchers attempting automated dependency confusion attacks for bounties, placing immense strain on registry maintainers and security analysts.

Defense Strategies: Package Firewalls and Enterprise Best Practices

To safeguard software development pipelines, organizations must adopt modern supply chain defenses:

Package Firewalls and Proxies: Deploying package firewalls that intercept npm and PyPI package requests, scanning package contents, publish age, metadata anomalies, and install scripts before packages reach developer machines.

Private Vetted Registries: Enforcing policies where internal builds only fetch approved, mirror-cached dependencies.

Outbound Egress Filtering: Monitoring and restricting egress traffic from developer environments and CI/CD runners to prevent unvetted webhook or C2 callbacks.

Key Takeaways and Open-Source Resources

McCarty concludes by urging organizations to invest in dedicated supply chain security expertise and provides open-source malware feeds, research repositories, and tracking resources (available on GitHub @sixmile) for threat researchers.

talks.title: Letthemin: Facilitating High Value Purple Teams Using Assumed Compromise
talks.teaser: A battle-tested assumed-compromise methodology for purple teaming that tests detection across the entire killchain.
talks.summary:
Introduction to Assumed Compromise Purple Teaming

Sarah Hume, Purple Team Service Lead at Security Risk Advisors (SRA), presents a refined, regimented, and repeatable methodology for conducting purple team assessments using an assumed compromise approach. While the definition of purple teaming varies across the cybersecurity community, Hume articulates how starting from an assumed initial breach enables security programs to maximize testing efficiency, uncover detection blind spots, and foster collaborative improvement between red and blue teams.

Defining the Core Philosophy: Flipping the Burden of Perfection

Traditional defensive posture suffers from the age-old dilemma where defenders must protect every possible asset 24/7, while an attacker only needs to succeed once. Hume advocates "flipping the burden of perfection" through the assumed compromise model. Rather than wasting days of assessment time attempting to penetrate external perimeter controls, organizations provision standard user credentials and endpoint access to the red team. Testing then focuses on traversing the complete attack lifecycle—from persistence and privilege escalation to defense evasion, lateral movement, credential access, and impact. Defenders do not need to prevent every isolated command; they only need to detect and disrupt enough links in the attack chain to break the adversary's progress.

Structuring an Assumed Compromise Engagement

The presentation details key operational assumptions required for a successful exercise:

Assume Controls Will Fail: Recognize that endpoint and network defenses can be bypassed by dedicated adversaries.

Assume Adversaries Will Find a Path: Focus on visibility and response rather than relying on perimeter fortifications.

Assume Another Control Can Be Added: Every test offers an opportunity to craft custom detection rules, hone configurations, or tighten access policies.

Assume Mutual Learning: Red and blue teams participate as equal partners with shared objectives.

Telemetry, Detection, and Prevention Parity

During live exercises, each executed technique is evaluated across three core criteria:

Telemetry Generation: Did the endpoint, network, or cloud sensors record the underlying activity in raw logs?

Alert / Detection Visibility: Did the SIEM, EDR, or SOC consoles trigger an actionable detection alert?

Prevention / Block: Did security controls automatically stop or neutralize the attack technique?

This structured scoring reveals whether a missing detection is due to a logging gap, a parsing error, or an alert threshold issue.

Eliminating Audit-Speak and Fostering True Collaboration

A critical factor in successful purple teaming is interpersonal dynamics and reporting language. Hume advises eliminating traditional audit terminology: avoid words like "failure" or "vulnerability ratings" (critical, high, medium, low), which trigger defensiveness from engineering teams. Instead, frame outcomes as "remediation project priorities" and "engineering tuning opportunities," ensuring all stakeholders remain engaged and motivated.

Tooling, Automation, and Longitudinal Improvement

For exercise execution and automation, Hume highlights the use of Mythic C2 alongside customized Jupyter notebooks to orchestrate multi-stage technique execution and data logging. Automated Breach and Attack Simulation tools and frameworks (like CALDERA) are recommended for continuous regression validation in between comprehensive, human-led purple team assessments.

Key Takeaways and Recommendations

Focus on the Full Killchain: Provision internal access to thoroughly test lateral movement, credential theft, and exfiltration defenses.

Involve Broader Stakeholders: Invite system administrators, engineers, and SOC analysts into the exercise room to observe live attacker techniques.

Drive Incremental Resilience: Measure longitudinal improvement across detection coverage, log quality, and incident response speed over successive engagements.

talks.title: Red Russians: How Russian APT Groups Follow Offensive Security Research
talks.teaser: How Russian state-sponsored APTs weaponize public red team tools and POCs within days of release.
talks.summary:
Introduction: The Offensive Research Dilemma

Will Thomas, seasoned cyber threat intelligence researcher, presents a deep dive into how Russian state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups actively track, adopt, and operationalize open-source offensive security research. While red team tools and public proof-of-concept (POC) exploits are created to help defenders validate and improve enterprise security controls, hostile intelligence services frequently repurpose these exact tools into active espionage campaigns—often within days or weeks of publication.

Russian Intelligence Services and APT Groups Profiled

Thomas maps out the landscape of Russian threat actors monitored in his research:

APT28 (Fancy Bear / Forest Blizzard): Associated with the Russian military intelligence agency (GRU Unit 26165), known for rapid exploit adoption and aggressive cyber-espionage.

APT29 (Cozy Bear / Midnight Blizzard): Attributed to the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), recognized for sophisticated, stealthy tradecraft targeting cloud environments, Microsoft 365, and supply chains.

Sandworm (Seashell Blizzard / GRU Unit 74455): Notorious for disruptive cyber warfare, operational technology attacks, and data wiping campaigns.

Turla (Waterbug / Venomous Bear): Aligned with the FSB, known for specialized covert implants and complex multi-stage infection chains.

Rapid Weaponization of Public Exploits and Tools

Thomas illustrates how threat actors systematically scan security blogs, conference presentations, and GitHub repositories for weaponizable material. Rather than expending resources developing bespoke exploits from scratch, Russian APTs leverage community tooling to reduce operational costs and blend in with legitimate red team assessments.

Case Studies: TeamsPhisher, ClickFix, and TeamCity

The presentation highlights several real-world examples of rapid tool adoption:

TeamsPhisher: Within days of the open-source release of this Microsoft Teams phishing automation utility, Russian actors integrated the tool into live campaigns targeting government and defense entities.

ClickFix Social Engineering: When researchers documented a novel social engineering lure that tricked users into running clipboard-injected PowerShell commands via the Windows Run dialog (Win+R / Ctrl+V) under the guise of solving a CAPTCHA, APT28 deployed the technique against Ukrainian targets within weeks.

TeamCity Pre-Auth RCE: Public POCs for JetBrains TeamCity server vulnerabilities were weaponized almost immediately by Russian state actors to compromise software development infrastructure.

The Russian APT Tool Matrix

To help defenders catalog and detect these threats, Thomas introduced the "Russian APT Tool Matrix" on GitHub. The matrix classifies tools across core MITRE ATT&CK tactical categories:

Credential Theft: Ubiquitous use of Mimikatz, AADInternals, and token extraction tools.

Defense Evasion: Drivers and utilities like EDRSandBlast to blind endpoint protection agents.

C2 and Post-Exploitation: Widespread adoption of Cobalt Strike, Impacket, Sliver, and cracked underground releases of Brute Ratel C4.

Discovery and Exfiltration: Scripted cloud API tools abusing legitimate services (Microsoft Graph API, OneDrive, Google Drive) for covert data exfiltration.

Threat Hunting and Detection Engineering Workflows

Thomas details a collaborative workflow uniting CTI, threat hunting, and security engineering teams. CTI analysts collect emerging tool releases and extract structural artifacts; threat hunters write hunting queries; and detection engineers deploy and refine alerts in SIEM and EDR platforms. Threat hunters must proactively emulate newly published offensive tools rather than waiting months for formal threat intelligence reports.

Key Takeaways for Red and Blue Teams

Think Before Publishing: Offensive researchers and red teamers must weigh the defensive benefit against the operational risks before open-sourcing fully automated exploit tooling on GitHub.

Detect Common Tradecraft: Blue teams must prioritize robust detection engineering against widely shared post-exploitation tools, living-off-the-land techniques, and script block logging.

Proactive Emulation: Incorporate newly disclosed adversary TTPs into threat hunting cycles immediately to prevent nation-state dwell time.

talks.title: Blurred Lines: Evolving Tactics of North Korean Cyber Threat Actors
talks.teaser: How North Korean threat groups share infrastructure, reallocate malware tools, and challenge traditional attribution.
talks.summary:
Introduction to North Korean Cyber Operations

Seongsu Park, Staff Threat Researcher at Zscaler ThreatLabz based in South Korea, delivers an extensive analysis of the evolving tactics, organizational structures, and attribution complexities surrounding North Korean (DPRK) state-sponsored cyber threat actors. Over the past decade, DPRK cyber capabilities have advanced from uncoordinated, rudimentary operations into a highly synchronized, state-directed cyber apparatus capable of complex espionage and large-scale financial theft.

The Complexity and Pitfalls of Cyber Attribution

Park explores the core challenges of threat actor attribution in modern cyber intelligence. Attribution relies on synthesizing digital artifacts, compilation timestamps, infrastructure patterns, language traits, and Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs). However, threat actors intentionally employ anti-attribution techniques, and analysts frequently fall into cognitive bias traps by attempting to categorize novel attack activity under rigid, historical threat group labels.

Case Study: Tool Handover and Developer Migration (PebbleDash to Kimsuky)

Park details a multi-year investigation illustrating how DPRK threat groups share toolsets and reallocate personnel:

PebbleDash and HTTP Spy: Historically, the PebbleDash malware family was exclusively associated with the Lazarus Group (Labyrinth Chollima). However, subsequent campaigns targeting South Korean defense contractors, aerospace firms, and heavy industry deployed PebbleDash alongside unique JavaScript-based infection chains typically attributed to Kimsuky (Velvet Chollima).

C2 Server Misconfigurations: Deep forensic analysis of a misconfigured adversary C2 server revealed backend PHP scripts managing spear-phishing templates and over 400 shortened URLs specifically designed to harvest South Korean portal credentials—a hallmark Kimsuky operation.

Organizational Reallocation: Park concludes that DPRK cyber units dynamically transfer custom malware code, developer talent, and operational responsibilities across sub-groups, blurring traditional boundaries between Lazarus and Kimsuky.

Emerging Threat Actors and Public Tool Exploitation

Park examines a recent cyber campaign that unfolded five days after the declaration of martial law in South Korea, demonstrating the agility of regional threat actors:

Topical Spear-Phishing: The attackers capitalized on intense media interest surrounding the political event to distribute spear-phishing files containing malicious Control Panel Applets (.CPL files).

Multi-Stage Chain via GitHub: The payload fetched archived components from attacker-controlled GitHub repositories, utilizing DLL search order hijacking to load an encrypted in-memory stage via Donut loader.

Public and Commodity Tool Integration: Rather than using proprietary implants, the actors leveraged publicly available tools, including ToaStealer, Cobalt Strike, and Godot-based loaders, complicating attribution.

Targeting Regional Software: The campaign specifically interacted with popular South Korean utilities (such as BandiZip) and exhibited working hours aligned with the GMT+8 and GMT+9 time zones.

Addressing Cognitive Bias in Threat Intelligence

Park shares vital lessons on overcoming confirmation bias during malware analysis. When researchers encounter familiar code snippets, they risk prematurely concluding attribution without analyzing the entire attack chain. Full-chain telemetry—spanning initial access lures, payload staging, in-process execution mechanisms, and C2 hosting—is mandatory for accurate threat intelligence.

Key Takeaways and Collaborative Defense

Dynamic Actor Structures: Nation-state actors operate like agile enterprises, reallocating tooling, developers, and infrastructure across campaigns.

Context-Driven Attribution: Focus on end-to-end operational context rather than isolated malware indicators.

Public-Private Cooperation: Effective defense against sophisticated state actors requires active threat sharing between private intelligence researchers, CERTs, and law enforcement agencies.

talks.title: Decision Making in Adversarial Automation
talks.teaser: Balancing stochastic LLMs and deterministic graph state engines to automate adversarial attack decisions.
talks.summary:
Introduction: Stochastic Parrots vs. Deterministic Predators

Bobby Kuzma and Michael Odell ("Moch") delve into the mathematical and algorithmic challenges of automated decision-making in adversarial cybersecurity environments. The speakers examine the contrasting paradigms between "stochastic parrots" (generative AI models that generate probabilistic text and decisions based on statistical correlations) and "deterministic predators" (systems designed to execute reproducible, deterministic attack strategies based on formal state verification).

The Mathematical Challenge of State and Action Spaces

Automating adversarial behavior in enterprise networks introduces extreme computational complexity:

State Space Explosion: Enterprise environments consist of tens of thousands of hosts, user accounts, services, permissions, and network routes. Modeling every potential system state creates a combinatorial explosion that exceeds manageable compute capacity.

Action Space Complexity: At any given moment, an automated agent can choose from thousands of potential tools, commands, and exploit parameters. Evaluating every state-action pair (Q-values) becomes intractable under traditional reinforcement learning without rigorous constraints.

Limitations of Rule-Based State Machines in Adversarial Testing

While traditional checklists and decision trees are algorithmically straightforward and explainable, they function as rigid state machines. In dynamic network environments, static decision trees fail to adapt when unexpected conditions arise, and their deterministic nature makes them easily predictable and signature-detectable by modern defense mechanisms.

Graph-Based Modeling and Subgraph Matching

To navigate massive network topologies efficiently, the speakers borrow graph theory principles popularized by BloodHound and financial fraud detection systems:

Property Graphs: Representing the target network, systems, credentials, and access relationships as rich property graphs.

Subgraph Matching: Instead of searching the entire graph at every step, automated engines evaluate whether local subgraphs meet the exact prerequisites required to execute a specific offensive technique.

Patterned Preconditions: Techniques and tools are modeled with explicit input requirements (e.g. valid SMB credentials, port 445 reachability, local admin rights) and expected outcome states.

Tooling Architecture: Property Graphs, DSL, and Kùzu

Kuzma and Odell introduce an open-source tooling architecture developed for deterministic TTP selection:

Domain Specific Language (DSL): A YAML-based DSL defining preconditions, graph query patterns, tool arguments, and graph transformations upon execution.

Embedded Graph Engine (Kùzu): Rather than deploying resource-heavy client-server graph databases like Neo4j, the architecture utilizes Kùzu—an open-source, embedded, in-process property graph database built for fast Cypher queries and analytical workloads.

Demonstration: Telemetry-Driven Attack Execution

The presenters demonstrate a live-recorded simulation where an operator executes basic reconnaissance commands (such as nmap and Linux enumeration). The engine ingests operator console telemetry in real time, continuously updates the local Kùzu property graph, evaluates matching subgraphs, and autonomously suggests the next optimal attack vector—guiding the workflow through hash extraction, hash cracking, and Active Directory domain dumping (secretsdump).

Key Takeaways and Future Horizons

Structure Before Automation: Effective adversarial automation requires robust, graph-based structural representations of target environments before applying AI or probabilistic logic.

Deterministic Explainability: Deterministic graph engines enable operators to explain exactly why a particular action was taken at any given second.

Open-Source Tooling: The speakers encourage the offensive and defensive communities to leverage their open-source DSL and embedded graph framework to build scalable, explainable security automation.

talks.title: Here and Now: Exploiting the Human Layer at the Right Moment
talks.teaser: Applying photojournalism principles and invisible theater to seize decisive moments in physical social engineering.
talks.summary:
Introduction: Beyond Rigid Pretexting

Daniel Isler, team lead for physical penetration testing and social engineering, delivers an engaging presentation on mastering physical social engineering through presence, timing, and situational awareness. Drawing inspiration from documentary photography pioneers like Margaret Bourke-White and Henri Cartier-Bresson, Isler argues that successful physical infiltration is not about executing rigid, rehearsed scripts, but about recognizing the "decisive moment" and adapting fluidly to environmental shifts.

The Perception-Evaluation-Decision-Action Framework

Isler introduces a continuous cognitive framework used by elite physical red teamers when operating in high-stakes environments:

Perceive: Actively observe sensory inputs—visual cues, body language, ambient conversations, uniforms, and security postures.

Evaluate: Rapidly assess whether the current situation aligns with the mission objectives or presents an immediate risk.

Decide: Determine whether to pivot the pretext, modify tone and persona, or seize an unexpected opening.

Act: Execute the decisive action calmly and naturally to produce the contextually required response.

Invisible Theater and Hemingway's Iceberg Theory

The talk draws profound parallels between physical penetration testing and dramatic art forms:

Invisible Theater (Augusto Boal): In the 1970s, Augusto Boal staged public scenes without announcing them as performances; bystanders accepted the scenario as reality because there were no artificial stage boundaries. Similarly, effective social engineers do not stand out as actors—they become part of the natural organizational flow.

Hemingway's Iceberg Theory: In literature, the dignity of an iceberg lies in only showing one-eighth of itself above water. In social engineering, what an operator chooses NOT to say is often more convincing than over-explaining. Allowing targets to fill in the blanks using their own assumptions creates unbreakable trust.

Case Study: Infiltrating a Corporate Headquarters and Server Room

Isler recounts a real-world physical intrusion into a heavily fortified corporate facility:

Encountering the Unexpected: Upon arriving at reception, the team faced a newly appointed floor manager ("Anna") whose name had not appeared in OSINT because the previous manager had resigned weeks prior.

Activating Implicit Validation: Rather than hesitating, the team presented locally hosted HTML email threads referencing corporate leadership. Anna welcomed the team, validating their presence without realizing she had done so.

The Server Room Standoff: Reaching the secure server room, a strict security guard became suspicious, held the team's badges, and reached for the phone to call security headquarters. In that exact fraction of a second, the team calmly suggested: "You can call Anna—she's in charge on this floor and can confirm our visit." Seeing the guard's micro-expression shift, the team let the silence work. The guard smiled, hung up the phone, and personally escorted the red team into the server room.

Operational Safety and the Rule of Three

Isler emphasizes the strict ethical and safety protocols governing professional physical red teaming:

Safety Cards: Always carry authorized letters of authorization and emergency contact details.

The Rule of Three: If a target challenges the team's pretext, make at most three non-confrontational attempts to de-escalate or convince them. If suspicion persists after three attempts, cease the attempt, disclose the assessment, and present the authorization letter safely.

Key Takeaways for Physical Security and Defense

Access is Seen, Not Forced: The most effective physical access paths exploit existing organizational behaviors rather than brute-forcing locks.

Train Staff on Contextual Verification: Organizations must train employees and security personnel to verify identity through independent channels rather than relying on phone numbers or names supplied on the spot.

Respect Operational Ethics: Maintain strict safety guidelines and respect human boundaries during every physical security engagement.

talks.title: Countering Forensics Software by Baiting Them
talks.teaser: Using Android honeytoken tripwires to trigger real-time data destruction against mobile forensics software.
talks.summary:
Introduction: The Blind Spot in Mobile Forensic Extraction

Assistant Professor Weihan Goh alongside researchers Joseph Lim and Isaac Soon present groundbreaking anti-forensic research exposing a critical blind spot in mobile digital forensics. While extensive research has examined methods for bypassing Android lock screens and gaining physical or logical access, digital forensics tools and law enforcement examiners operate under the fundamental assumption that once access is established, the mobile operating system and file extraction pipeline remain passive, truthful, and cooperative. The research demonstrates how adversarially modified Android environments can deploy stealthy countermeasure tripwires to silently corrupt, encrypt, or manipulate evidence in real time during extraction.

Understanding Logical Extraction and the MTP Protocol

Digital forensic extraction workflows frequently rely on logical acquisition over the Media Transfer Protocol (MTP) or Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to acquire files from shared internal and external storage. Forensics software suites—such as Cellebrite UFED / Physical Analyzer, Magnet AXIOM, and Belkasoft Evidence Center X—perform bulk, deterministic directory traversals starting from root directories or alphabetical folder listings, retrieving files sequentially without verifying whether filesystem access events trigger active background services.

The Honeytoken Baiting Mechanism on Android

The researchers developed an active anti-forensics architecture leveraging decoy files ("honeytokens") and filesystem tripwires:

Honeytoken Placement: Bait files are positioned in predictable top-level directories (e.g. /sdcard/Download or shared storage root) that commercial extraction tools invariably inspect early during their traversal routine.

Filesystem Observers (inotify): A lightweight background service monitors file descriptor events using the Linux inotify API via Android FileObserver services.

Real-Time Payload Triggering: The moment a forensic tool reads or opens the honeytoken file, the tripwire fires an automated payload that immediately encrypts or securely overwrites sensitive "crown jewel" assets (such as encrypted chat databases, SMS logs, contacts, photos, and credentials) before the forensic tool can reach those directories.

Proof of Concept: Defeating Cellebrite, Belkasoft, and Magnet AXIOM

The researchers showcase live recorded demonstrations against three premier commercial forensic solutions:

Cellebrite UFED: As Cellebrite initiated logical file extraction over MTP, touching the bait file triggered background AES encryption. The resulting Cellebrite extraction report contained only ciphertext for sensitive target databases, completely denying usable evidence to the examiner.

Belkasoft Evidence Center X: Belkasoft's top-down shared storage acquisition immediately triggered the inotify observer, encrypting crown jewel files before acquisition finished.

Magnet AXIOM: By utilizing a larger padding file in target directories to create a deliberate time buffer, the background observer successfully encrypted all designated documents and databases while Magnet AXIOM processed the acquisition queue.

Implications and Defensive Countermeasures for Forensic Examiners

The authors discuss crucial procedural adjustments for forensic investigators and software vendors:

Avoid Unverified Bulk Acquisition: Forensic examiners must reconsider relying on automated bulk MTP extractions on suspect devices.

Selective and Prioritized Extraction: Extract critical artifacts first rather than following predictable alphabetical or hierarchical paths.

Cold-System / Chip-Off Forensics: Where feasible, utilize physical memory dumps, EDL mode, or chip-off extraction to prevent device CPUs from executing running anti-forensics processes.

Forensic Tool Verification: Forensic vendors must evaluate how their tools behave within active, adversarially modified target environments.

Key Takeaways and Future Research

Device Access is Only the Beginning: Gaining physical or logical access to an Android device does not guarantee evidentiary integrity.

Active Countermeasures Pose Severe Investigative Risks: Automated, real-time tripwires can silently subvert chain of custody and forensic accuracy.

Need for Rigorous Forensic Testing: The digital forensics community must develop defenses against active anti-forensic techniques that exploit deterministic acquisition workflows.

talks.title: TotalTest Simulations 2 Oh! From Exploits to Economics
talks.teaser: Transforming breach simulations from technical point tests into quantified economic value for executive leadership.
talks.summary:
Introduction: Shifting From Exploits to Economics

Nebu Varghese, Senior Director in the Cybersecurity Practice at FTI Consulting, presents a strategic framework for elevating offensive security from technical exploit discovery to quantifiable business economics. Addressing the common challenge where executive leadership views red teaming and penetration testing merely as recurring operational cost centers, Varghese unveils "TotalTest"—a metrics-driven simulation methodology designed to translate technical breach simulations into defensible financial risk reduction and return on security investment (ROSI).

Why Point-in-Time Penetration Testing Fails Modern Enterprises

Traditional penetration testing models suffer from severe structural limitations:

Point-in-Time Snapshots: An annual or semi-annual penetration test provides only a temporary snapshot of vulnerabilities, quickly invalidated by ongoing infrastructure changes, software deployments, and novel threat tactics.

Focus on Vulnerability Counts: Reporting long lists of CVEs without contextual operational impact fails to communicate true enterprise risk to board members and Chief Financial Officers.

Lack of Business Alignment: Security leaders struggle to articulate how finding a specific domain escalation path or implant execution capability directly protects revenue, preserves supply chain uptime, or optimizes insurance premiums.

The TotalTest Simulation Framework Architecture

The TotalTest methodology integrates continuous, intelligence-led adversary emulation with enterprise risk quantification:

Scenario Design: Multi-phase simulation scenarios modeled on relevant sector threat intelligence, exercising full attack paths across IT, OT, and cloud boundaries.

Operational Telemetry: Capturing detailed metrics on time-to-detect (TTD), time-to-respond (TTR), lateral movement dwell time, and defensive mitigation efficacy.

Iterative Cycles: Running recurring, targeted simulation cycles to measure continuous improvement over time rather than isolated one-off assessments.

Quantifying Revenue Protected and Loss Reduction

Varghese demonstrates a financial modeling methodology for converting simulation results into revenue protected:

Defining Fixed and Variable Breach Costs: Establishing base financial impacts for enterprise downtime, incident response recovery, regulatory fines, and operational disruption.

Measuring Loss Reduction per Cycle: Demonstrating how shortening dwell time and improving detection reduces expected breach loss (e.g. modeling how reducing recovery downtime saves hundreds of thousands of dollars in potential incident impact).

Demonstrating ROSI to the Board: Providing quantifiable ratios (such as proving that every dollar invested in targeted simulation controls protects nearly double that value in financial risk safeguard).

Industry Benchmarking and Optimizing Cyber Insurance

A critical advantage of the TotalTest framework is enabling defensible executive benchmarking:

Empirical Industry Data: Incorporating industry telemetry from sources such as the Verizon DBIR and IBM Cost of a Data Breach reports, layered with sector-specific threat intelligence to establish realistic baseline breach costs.

Cyber Insurance Premium Optimization: Presenting verified simulation data to cyber underwriters to demonstrate robust risk controls, thereby negotiating lower insurance premiums and higher coverage terms.

Operating Within Risk Appetite: Giving the board a clear, data-driven trajectory showing how security initiatives systematically reduce residual risk toward board-approved risk tolerance thresholds.

Key Takeaways and Multi-Tiered Organizational Feedback

Simulations Feed All Security Disciplines: Technical findings from simulations must provide structured feedback to vulnerability management (re-calibrating prioritization), the SOC (tuning high-fidelity use cases), and CTI (validating threat hunting hypotheses).

Speak the Language of the C-Suite: Transform technical offensive findings into financial metrics that CFOs, CEOs, and board committees understand.

Test Smarter, Break Smarter, Fund Fixes: Utilize continuous, economic-driven simulations to turn security from a perceived cost center into a tangible competitive advantage.
